newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway gains more than UK from Frigg deal - report.
newsitem.headline: Norway gains more than UK from Frigg deal - report.

text.p: Norway could deliver between six and seven billion cubic metres per year of gas to Britain by the end of the decade following the agreement in April by the two governments over the Frigg Treaty, industry analysts Wood Mackenzie said on Thursday.
Woodmac said Norwegian gas exports to Britain could be "significantly greater" if additional compression facilities are installed for the Norwegian Frigg pipeline.

"UK gas has always had access to the Norwegian pipeline on a negotiated basis and as a result the revised Frigg Treaty does not appear to significantly affect UK producers, whereas it represents a major new export opportunity for producers in Norway," Woodmac said in a special review.
The report said Norway has access to large volumes of unsold gas, which is creating a log-jam of new gas developments competing for gas sales contracts.

If new gas sales were to arise in Britain, several fields in the northern sector of the Norwegian North Sea, including Huldra, Kvitebjoern and Oseberg, could be potential candidates to supply gas due to their proximity to Frigg, Woodmac said.
"Moreover, these fields could be readily tied into the Frigg pipeline by 1999/2000 which coincides with the likely emergence of a significant supply shortfall in the UK market."

But the scale of any new gas sales to Britain and the choice of fields to supply them would have to fit in with the Norwegian authority's overall strategy for gas sales, which depend upon Norway's other commitments to continental Europe, the gas price differential between Britain and the continent and the impact of the start up of deliveries through the Interconnector.
"The UK-continent Interconnector will act both as a safety valve for surplus volumes of UK gas, and as a control on the pricing behaviour of Norwegian exporters," Woodmac said.
